chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Shu'ayb ibn Abdillah from one of his companions, raising it, said:

A man came to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) and said, 'O Commander of the Faithful! Advise me of an aspect of righteousness by which I may attain salvation.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'O questioner! Listen, then understand, then be convinced, then act; and know that people are of three types: an ascetic, a patient one, and a covetous one.'
As for the ascetic, grief and happiness have exited his heart, so he does not rejoice in anything from the world, nor does he despair over anything from it that has left him; thus he is at peace.

As for the patient one, he wishes for it in his heart; but when he attains from it, he restrains his self from it due to its evil consequence and its repulsiveness. If you were to look into his heart, you would be astonished by its chastity, humility, and resoluteness.

As for the covetous one, he does not care from where the world comes to him, whether from its permissible means or its prohibited means, and he does not care what filth he has incurred in it, destroyed his soul, and lost his manliness; thus they are in a flood of confusion, tossing about.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful; title for Imam Ali
key_terms.الدُّنْيَا: The world; worldly life and its pleasures
key_terms.رَاغِبٌ: Covetous; one who eagerly seeks worldly gain regardless of source
key_terms.زَاهِدٌ: Ascetic; one who has detached from worldly emotions
key_terms.صَابِرٌ: Patient; one who restrains self-desire despite longing

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of people according to Imam Ali in this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi presents a nuanced tripartite classification of human spiritual states, distinguishing between the ascetic (zāhid) who has transcended worldly attachment, the patient (ṣābir) who controls desire through foresight of the Hereafter, and the covetous (rāhib) who pursues worldly gain indiscriminately. Scholarly commentary often highlights this as a practical guide for self-assessment, emphasizing that true righteousness requires not just action but the purification of the heart's relationship with the transient world. The opening instruction to 'listen, ask, be convinced, then act' underscores the Shia epistemological emphasis on verified knowledge preceding practice.
